It's not an accident or an oversight that we the readers do not know by the end of the story whether or not Gregor actually did turn into some sort of bug - it's part of the point of the story. According to his account, he did, and according to his account, others responded to him in ways that he perceived to mean that they recognized it just as he did. It was what he saw in himself and it was what he saw mirrored in the reactions of others to him, therefore he believed it to be so. I started out as a kid on the JVNC.net and had what may have been the last working email address there. I've watched personal computing, personal communication, the Internet, and the sub-cultures they all catalyzed evolve. I think we're still in the early days of the Internet's story. I look forward to the development of the Semantic Web, social-semantic platforms, open social VR platforms, robot, agent, and infrastructure networking, the realization of the ubiquitous computing vision through the evolution of dynamic VPNs or 'personal domains', and the evolution of blockchain technology into a globally distributed virtual cloud computing environment. Social networking may have reached its saturation point and I see sites like Reddit and Twitter struggling with deep philosophical and ethical contradictions. It's time for new models and metaphors, but they're not likely coming from what is now a web media 'establishment'. Much of the world doesn't know the difference between the Internet and Facebook, and I find that understandable yet still disturbing.

Once convergent, personal computing and mobile communications now seem divergent with mobile device use--and more importantly mobile culture--beginning to supercede the personal computer as personal computing has become stuck in old architectures, tired interface metaphors, and intractable learning curves, too weighted down by the drag of old code and vested interests to evolve as rapidly. The computer is 'commodifying' and minimalism has reduced product design to a numbers game; speed, memory capacity, screen size/resolution, weight and thinness, battery life. How many ways can you really differentiate the physical design of one smartphone, tablet, or laptop from another as they all approach an ergonomic optimum and dimensional minimum? All that distinguishes products is the on-screen aesthetics and experience of a given system platform--and those too are becoming self-similar the more refined as true experimentation declines. While generally panned, I was very interested in the Solu computer simply because it, very bravely, explores a very new user interface metaphor and operability model. The first truly new one in decades. (it has issues you'd expect from something new and needs better thought-out wireless connectivity and wireless charging, but it's more novel than anything else right now. It's a look at how the smartphone and personal computer could have converged in a ubiquitous cloud computing environment but didn't because of the silo mentality still common to the computing and communications industries. We're still talking about phone companies, for christ sake!)
